text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Working hours should be cut by two hours a week within the next five years, according to Prime Minister Goran Persson. This was the strongest line to come out of the Social Democrats party committee meeting this week.
- One of Sweden's most shocking murders, the 1989 killing of 10-year-old Helen Nilsson from Horby, could be solved. Police have arrested a 43-year-old man from Horby suspected of her murder.

- Swedish media family the Bonniers plan to sell Semic International to Denmark's Egmont group, the paper says. Semic was set up in 1950 under the name Serieforlaget and has produced the Phantom and other popular comics in Sweden.

- Volvo has introduced a new city jeep to its V70 range, called the V70 XC. It is designed for the U.S. market with higher and thicker jeep-like tyres. It will be the most expensive of the Volvo models and production will start this autumn.

- State-owned property group Vasakronan is selling 194 properties worth about five billion crowns to a consortium involving international investment bank Credit Suisse First Boston. A letter of intent has already been written up.

- Drug company Astra said it had received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its asthma treatment, the Pulmicort Turbuhaler. It will be launched in the U.S. this autumn and the company said it will become the leading asthma drug in the U.S..
- Sweden's biggest share administrator, SPP Kapitalforvaltning, has decided not to sell Swedish funds in its new offer of a so-called unit-linked fund, opting instead for overseas funds.

- Swedish telecommunications company Telia has vastly improved its Infomedia Response service over the past seven months under the guidance of Ingrid Engstrom. Turnover has increased to 2.7 billion crowns a year from one billion crowns in 1996. Staff numbers have been cut and efficiency raised.
